sceneAlt: A small corner shop seen from the front: on the left a checkout with a till, a conveyor belt, a chocolate bar and a paper bag, and a shopping basket on the floor. At the back a tall shelf with wine, milk, juice, eggs, toilet paper, a roast chicken, sausages, cheese, a watermelon, a tomato and a present; beside it a hanging scale under a bakery shelf with a cake and a croissant. On the right a chest freezer with ice cream, a steak and a fish; in front a fruit and vegetable stall, a bucket of flowers and a shopping trolley.
help.hook: A small corner shop full of groceries: find each item in the picture, then give it its article.
help.intro: A picture hunt instead of a deck: one small corner shop with 32 things to find in it, all words you need when you go shopping — der Einkaufswagen, die Kasse, das Fließband, the cheese on the shelf and the fish in the freezer. The prompt asks Wo ist …? and you tap the object in the picture. A tap on bare wall or floor costs nothing; a tap on the wrong object tells you what you hit and you keep looking, and after three misses the right one is shown. Each find shows its label, coloured by its gender (blue der, red die, green das), then leaves a small tick in that colour, so you can see what you have already found. Once you have passed a run, the hunt turns harder: the prompt hides the article (Wo ist ___ Kasse?), and after the find you choose der, die or das yourself. No object is asked twice in the same run.
help.tips[0].title: Compounds in the corner shop: the last part decides
help.tips[0].text: Shop words are often compounds, and the last part decides the article. Einkauf + Wagen: der Wagen, so der Einkaufswagen. Kühl + Truhe: die Truhe, so die Kühltruhe. Look at the end of the word.
help.tips[0].check.why: The last part is der Strauß, so the whole word is der Blumenstrauß.
help.tips[1].title: Words in -e are usually die — but der Käse
help.tips[1].text: Most fruit and vegetables here end in -e and are feminine: die Tomate, die Gurke, die Banane, die Melone. The same goes for die Waage, die Tüte and die Kasse. The big exception sits on the shelf: der Käse.
help.tips[1].check.why: Käse ends in -e but is masculine: der Käse. It is the classic exception to the -e rule.
help.tips[2].title: -chen is always das
help.tips[2].text: A word made small with -chen is always neuter, whatever it means: das Hähnchen (a small Hahn) sits on the shelf. Watch out for der Kuchen on the bakery shelf: it only looks like a -chen word, it is not a small form of anything, and it is masculine.
help.tips[2].check.why: Words made small with -chen are always neuter: das Hähnchen. (die Hähnchen is the plural.)
help.remember[0]: The last part of a compound sets the article: der Wagen → der Einkaufswagen.
help.remember[1]: Most words in -e are die (die Tomate, die Tüte), but der Käse is masculine.
help.remember[2]: -chen is das: das Hähnchen — but der Kuchen.
